clinicalPearls: Rare autosomal dominant dysplasia caused by activating (gain-of-function) mutations in FGFR1 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 1).
Recognised by a clinical triad of craniosynostosis with a distinctive facies, rhizomelic short stature, and multiple radiolucent metaphyseal fibrous lesions.
The name means hollowed or carved bone, referring to the punched-out, non-ossifying-fibroma-like metaphyseal defects that hollow out the long bones.
Craniofacial features include a prominent forehead, midface hypoplasia, a depressed nasal bridge and proptosis.
The dental hallmark is failure of tooth eruption, with unerupted or impacted teeth and gingival overgrowth.
Fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) excess from the fibrous bone lesions can drive renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphataemia (interpreted qualitatively).
It belongs to the same receptor family as achondroplasia (FGFR3) and Pfeiffer syndrome (FGFR1/FGFR2) but is a distinct FGFR1 phenotype.
Most cases are sporadic (de novo dominant mutations), although vertical transmission is documented.
reference.pathophysiology: Osteoglophonic dysplasia is caused by heterozygous gain-of-function missense mutations in FGFR1, the gene encoding fibroblast growth factor receptor 1. Enhanced, ligand-independent FGFR1 signalling disturbs endochondral ossification, producing rhizomelic dwarfism; promotes premature fusion of the cranial sutures, causing craniosynostosis and the characteristic facies; and impairs bone remodelling, giving rise to the multiple non-ossifying, fibrous, radiolucent metaphyseal lesions that hollow out the long bones. Some of these fibrous lesions overproduce fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), a phosphaturic hormone, so that a subset of patients develop renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphataemia, analogous to tumour-induced osteomalacia. The failure of tooth eruption reflects the disordered bone and dental matrix around developing teeth. FGFR1 lies within the same receptor tyrosine kinase family as FGFR3 (mutated in achondroplasia) and FGFR2, and the osteoglophonic phenotype is distinguished from the other FGFR-related craniosynostosis syndromes by the combination of rhizomelia and the diagnostic hollowed metaphyseal lesions. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, with most probands carrying de novo mutations.
additionalDifferentials: Achondroplasia and hypochondroplasia (FGFR3) for the rhizomelic short stature
Other FGFR craniosynostosis syndromes: Pfeiffer, Crouzon and Apert (FGFR1/FGFR2)
Cleidocranial dysplasia (RUNX2) for delayed or failed tooth eruption
Fibrous dysplasia and McCune-Albright syndrome (GNAS) for lytic/fibrous bone lesions
Isolated non-ossifying fibromas and benign fibrous cortical defects
Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome (multiple non-ossifying fibromas with extraskeletal features)
Hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets (PHEX and other FGF23-related forms) for the phosphate wasting
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey demonstrating the radiolucent metaphyseal lesions and rhizomelia
Skull imaging or CT to assess the cranial sutures and craniosynostosis
Serum phosphate, calcium and alkaline phosphatase with assessment of renal phosphate handling (interpreted qualitatively); FGF23 where available
Orthopantomogram and dental imaging for unerupted and impacted teeth
FGFR1 molecular genetic testing by targeted analysis or gene panel
Ophthalmology review and, where indicated, neuroimaging for raised intracranial pressure
redFlags: Signs of raised intracranial pressure from multisuture craniosynostosis
Visual compromise from proptosis or optic nerve involvement
Symptomatic hypophosphataemia with bone pain, deformity or fractures
Airway obstruction or feeding difficulty from midface hypoplasia in infancy
reference.prognosis: The outlook is variable: stature is reduced and craniofacial and dental problems are lifelong, but with coordinated craniofacial, orthopaedic, dental and metabolic (phosphate) care, outcomes and life expectancy are generally reasonable. The principal complications relate to raised intracranial pressure, vision and phosphate wasting.
pitfalls: Mistaking the metaphyseal lesions for isolated non-ossifying fibromas or fibrous dysplasia and missing the underlying syndrome
Overlooking FGF23-mediated hypophosphataemia as a treatable contributor to bone disease
Attributing the short stature to achondroplasia without recognising the craniofacial, dental and metaphyseal-lesion pattern
Failing to detect raised intracranial pressure in the setting of craniosynostosis
references: Nosology and classification of genetic skeletal disorders
Metabolic bone and endocrinology reference texts
management: Correction of hypophosphataemia driven by FGF23 excess with oral phosphate supplementation and an active vitamin D metabolite such as alfacalcidol or calcitriol
Cranial vault surgery for craniosynostosis, with monitoring and treatment of raised intracranial pressure
Orthopaedic management of the metaphyseal fibrous lesions, long-bone deformity and short stature
Dental and maxillofacial care for unerupted or impacted teeth and gingival overgrowth
Ophthalmology review for proptosis and neuroimaging where raised intracranial pressure is suspected
Coordinated multidisciplinary craniofacial, orthopaedic, dental and metabolic follow-up
Genetic counselling for the autosomal dominant gain-of-function FGFR1 mutation, with family assessment
